attacks.claim: On any SES batch error (including throttling, the expected failure mode) the loop records every recipient as a permanent failure and continues without retry, so transient errors silently drop subscribers from the issue and report them to publishers as 'Not delivered'.
attacks.evidence: if err != nil { for _, r := range batch.Recipients { failures.Record(ctx, batch.IssueID, r.SubscriberID, errCode(err)) } metrics.Inc("send.batch_failed"); continue }

attacks.claim: Production runs 48 workers at ~25 msg/s each (~1,200 msg/s theoretical) against a 300 msg/s SES account limit, so throttling is expected at launch, and that throttling is recorded as permanent recipient loss with no backoff or rate limiting.
attacks.evidence: SEND_WORKERS=48 · BATCH_SIZE=50 · SES production account limits (us-east-1): 300 messages/second, 25M/day

attacks.claim: The QA pass that supports the go-live claims ran with SES throttling simulated off, on a staging account capped at 14 msg/s where real 4-worker runs were throttled. The 11-minute, zero-failure result therefore does not reflect production SES behaviour, and no throttling-path test is listed.
attacks.evidence: Worker count capped at 4 in staging | — | Staging SES account limit is 14 msg/s; 4 workers were throttled intermittently, so QA ran with SES throttling simulated off via the sandbox mock

attacks.claim: The '14 min to under 3 min' goal and the public 'up to 5× faster' claim have no production-config measurement behind them; the only timing is an 11-minute single-issue run on 4 workers under simulated throttling, and 14→3 is about 4.7×, not 5×.
attacks.evidence: "Goal: cut median time-to-inbox for a 50k-subscriber issue from 14 min to under 3 min." / "Starting today, every Inkwell issue reaches inboxes up to 5× faster."

attacks.claim: The launch post tells all publishers Smart Send Time is live for every publication today at 100% default-on, which contradicts the 5%→25%→100% cohort ramp and the open-rate and late-ticket gates, and cannot be recalled once sent.
attacks.evidence: "ramp `SMART_SEND_DEFAULT` by publication cohort: 5% (week 1), 25% (week 2), 100% (week 3)" vs. "Smart Send Time is live for every publication today ... Nothing to set up; it's already on."

attacks.claim: Smart Send Time holds issues up to 18 hours by default for all publications, including the ~40% that publish time-sensitive news. Rollback releases only still-held issues, so breaking-news, election, and weather issues already delayed cannot be recovered.
attacks.evidence: "Enabled by default for all publications" and "Issues are held for at most 18 hours"; "4,480 of them (40%) are news or local-news outlets whose issues are time-sensitive"; rollback: "held issues are released immediately."

attacks.claim: The 71% Smart Send accuracy figure has no baseline and no pre-launch evidence that predicted timing beats the default, yet the launch post promises delivery 'when each reader is most likely to open it'.
attacks.evidence: "Smart Send Time: predicted hour within ±1h of actual top open hour, 2,000 sampled subscribers | — | 71%" / "we'll deliver each issue when each reader is most likely to open it."

attacks.claim: SES per-entry results are mapped to recipients by index with no length check, so a count or order mismatch misattributes failures to the wrong subscribers with no guard or metric.
attacks.evidence: for i, res := range out.BulkEmailEntryResults { ... batch.Recipients[i].SubscriberID ...

attacks.claim: Batch ack and retry semantics are unspecified: failed batches are skipped with `continue` before Ack, so their redelivery behaviour on crash or restart is undefined, risking duplicate sends or silent loss.
attacks.evidence: if err != nil { ... continue } ... q.Ack(ctx, batch) — no retry, dead-letter, or redelivery path shown for failed batches

attacks.claim: Smart Send hold has no timeout alerting, expiry-miss metric, or held-issue backlog alarm, and the on-call pager does not cover held-issue age.
attacks.evidence: On-call pager: queue lag > 10 min, complaint rate > 0.1%.

attacks.claim: Failure records are written one row at a time inside the loop, so a failed 50-recipient batch issues 50 synchronous DB writes exactly when the system is degraded.
attacks.evidence: for _, r := range batch.Recipients { failures.Record(ctx, batch.IssueID, r.SubscriberID, errCode(err)) }

attacks.claim: Pipeline v2 goes to 100% of sends on day one, with no percentage-based rollout to cap blast radius across all 11,240 publications.
attacks.evidence: Send pipeline v2: deploy Monday 09:00 UTC to 100% of sends; keep the Sidekiq sender deployed but idle for 14 days.

attacks.claim: No alerting on SES throttle rate, send_failures volume, or the 'Not delivered' count, so throttling-driven silent exclusion would not page on-call.
attacks.evidence: On-call pager: queue lag > 10 min, complaint rate > 0.1%.

attacks.claim: If SES accepted a batch but returned an error, those recipients are recorded as undelivered and excluded, with no reconciliation path for clearing the exclusions.
attacks.evidence: failures.Record(...errCode(err)) inside if err != nil, followed by continue; "those recipients are excluded from the issue's remaining sends"

attacks.claim: Rollback to the Sidekiq sender does not address state v2 wrote to Postgres (send_failures exclusions, ack state); a mid-issue switch could double-send or skip recipients.
attacks.evidence: "Rollback (pipeline): set `SENDER=sidekiq` in the dispatcher; in-flight batches drain in < 2 min." — ABSENT: compatibility of v2-written state with the Sidekiq sender

attacks.claim: Time-zone handling for Smart Send is unspecified, even though time-zone-aware scheduling was the top customer request; predicted hours could be computed in UTC and mis-timed for local readers, with no QA covering it.
attacks.evidence: Top customer request in Q3: scheduled sends with time zone support (shipped in 2026.08).
